expert_diagnosis: Lehman Brothers faced a fatal combination of excessive leverage, illiquid and overvalued real-estate and mortgage assets, and total dependence on short-term wholesale funding. The Bear Stearns rescue in March 2008 demonstrated that confidence-driven liquidity collapses could happen rapidly. Lehman's capital raise in June 2008 was insufficient to address the scale of the balance-sheet problem and delayed decisive restructuring. Management's public assertions of adequate liquidity were not supported by the underlying asset quality or funding structure. The core failure was the refusal to take decisive, credible action early enough to restore confidence — specifically, raising substantially more capital, recognising losses transparently, selling risky assets at realistic prices, or securing a strategic transaction before market confidence fully collapsed.
expert_first_action: Immediately pursue the largest feasible capital raise or asset disposal, accept realistic loss recognition on distressed holdings, and initiate a formal strategic process for a buyer or government-facilitated solution — before funding confidence collapses rather than after.
actual_decision: Lehman management continued to assert adequate liquidity and capital adequacy through summer 2008. Capital raise in June 2008 was insufficient in scale. Asset sales and leverage reduction were insufficient and delayed. No strategic buyer was secured and no government backstop was arranged before the filing.
harmful_actions: Continued public assertions of adequate liquidity when underlying asset quality and funding structure remained fragile
Insufficient capital raise relative to scale of balance-sheet stress
Delayed and inadequate asset sales at a time when markets were still open for transactions
Failed to secure a strategic buyer or government-facilitated solution before confidence collapsed
Delayed transparent loss recognition on real-estate and mortgage portfolios
beneficial_actions: Announced capital raise in June 2008, which was a directionally correct but insufficiently scaled action
citation: Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission, The Financial Crisis Inquiry Report (2011), available at https://fraser.stlouisfed.org/files/docs/historical/fct/fcic/fcic_final_report_full.pdf; Lehman Brothers 10-Q filed with SEC, June 2008; Anton R. Valukas, Examiner's Report, In re Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc., Bankr. S.D.N.Y. (2010).
actual_outcome: Lehman Brothers filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on September 15, 2008. The collapse was the largest bankruptcy filing in US history and became a pivotal event in the global financial crisis, triggering severe market dislocation across equity, credit, and money markets worldwide. The bankruptcy examiner's report identified excessive leverage, asset overvaluation, and inadequate loss recognition as central failures. Barclays subsequently acquired Lehman's North American investment banking and capital markets business out of bankruptcy.
documented_root_causes: Excessive leverage relative to thin equity base
Heavy exposure to illiquid and uncertain real-estate and mortgage assets
Short-term funding dependence in conditions of fragile market confidence
Inadequate and delayed loss recognition on distressed asset portfolios
Failure to raise sufficient capital or execute decisive asset disposals before confidence collapse
No strategic buyer or government backstop secured in time
Confidence-driven liquidity collapse once counterparty trust failed
final_business_state: Total collapse. Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc. filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy on September 15, 2008. The filing triggered global financial market dislocation. Core business units were sold to Barclays and Nomura in post-bankruptcy transactions. The event became the defining moment of the 2008 global financial crisis.
